messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 63
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Doctor
- Trauma Type: Terrorism
- Pcl5: 35

He is 63, a married North American man who has spent most of his adult life practicing medicine, and he carries himself with the careful composure of someone accustomed to being needed. When he first speaks about the event, he does so in the same measured tone he might use with a colleague, as if precision can keep the memory contained. But as the story unfolds, it becomes clear that the attack he survived has not stayed in the past. It continues to arrive in fragments, intruding into ordinary moments and altering the way he moves through the world.

The terrorist attack happens while he is traveling for a medical conference in a large city. He remembers the weather, the crowded streets, the ordinary feeling of walking between commitments with a half-finished cup of coffee in hand. Then the blast comes, abrupt and senseless, followed by screaming, smoke, and a violence so immediate that his mind struggles to organize it. He drops to the ground without thinking, instinct taking over before thought can catch up. In the minutes afterward, he is not a doctor but a body trying to survive. He sees shoes scattered on the pavement, notices a shoe with no person attached, and later cannot shake that image. He helps a wounded stranger with pressure on a bleeding wound, but his own hands shake so badly that he doubts whether he is helping at all. He is aware, with a sickening clarity, that this is the kind of scene he has only ever encountered in the abstract, in war reports and emergency planning discussions, not in his own life.

In the days after, he returns home physically intact but altered in ways his family can see before he can name them. He does not sleep. When he does drift off, he wakes with his heart pounding and his body drenched in sweat, certain for a few seconds that another explosion has occurred. He becomes preoccupied with entrances, exits, and the sound of engines idling outside the house. In the clinic, he keeps his manner steady with patients, but his concentration slips. He finds himself rereading charts, losing his place in conversations, and needing to excuse himself to the restroom when a hallway door slams too hard. He hates how quickly his body reacts, how it betrays him with a surge of adrenaline before he has even understood what he is hearing.

He begins avoiding news coverage, crowds, unfamiliar cities, even family outings that might involve long lines or packed public spaces. He offers practical reasons at first—he is busy, tired, behind on work—but his wife notices that his refusals come too quickly, with a flatness that feels different from mere preference. He stops sitting near windows in restaurants. He chooses seats that allow him to see the room. He scans people’s hands, their bags, the spaces around parked vehicles. These habits come so automatically that he only realizes how tense he has become when his shoulders ache at the end of the day.

What unsettles him most is the way his mind returns to the dead and injured. He thinks about the strangers he saw on the pavement and about whether he did enough in those first chaotic minutes. As a physician, he has spent his life acting decisively in crisis, and he cannot reconcile that identity with the helplessness he felt there. He replays the scene while driving, while shaving, while trying to listen at dinner. Sometimes a siren in the distance or the smell of diesel can pull him back so suddenly that he has to stop and orient himself, embarrassed by the force of it. He does not cry easily, but he becomes more irritable, more impatient, and more withdrawn. His wife says he seems present and absent at the same time.

Over time, he continues working, though not without strain. He remains committed to his patients, and his professionalism is intact, but it costs him more energy than it used to. He arrives early, checks locks without thinking, and sits with his back to the wall in meeting rooms. He is aware that he is bracing for something he cannot predict. At home, he tries to be reassuring, but his family has learned to read the brief tightening around his mouth when a loud sound startles him or when a televised blast scene appears without warning.

He speaks less about vulnerability than he once did, but beneath his restraint is a grief he is still trying to understand: grief for the people who died, for the world that had seemed orderly, and for the version of himself who believed that clinical knowledge offered some protection from randomness. He knows the event happened in a matter of seconds, yet its echo has stretched across months, shaping the way he sleeps, works, and moves through ordinary life with a quiet, constant vigilance.
